abstract: >
  RAPID (Risk of Attribute Prediction-Induced Disclosure) measures how many
  records of an original data set an attacker can infer a sensitive value for,
  using a model fitted on a released synthetic or anonymized data set. This
  vignette shows how to declare the attack, how to compute RAPID for a
  categorical and a numeric sensitive variable with `rapid()`, and how to
  read the result: the chance level, the excess over it, tests and intervals,
  the choice of the threshold, holdout records, the choice of the attacker,
  the contribution of each quasi-identifier and the cross-validation of a
  synthesizer. A section on practice says how to read and report a result and
  covers missing values, seeds and pitfalls. The last two sections list what
  changed from riskutility 0.2.0 and how to reproduce the paper.

```{r setup, include=FALSE}
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>",
  fig.width = 6,
  fig.height = 4,
  warning = TRUE,
  message = FALSE
)
library(riskutility)
has_rpart <- requireNamespace("rpart", quietly = TRUE)
f3 <- function(x) sprintf("%.3f", x)
f0 <- function(x) sprintf("%.0f", x)
pct <- function(x) sprintf("%.1f %%", 100 * x)
```

# The attack scenario {#sec-scenario}

What does the attacker know, and what does RAPID count? A data holder releases a synthetic or
anonymized version of a confidential data set. The attacker knows a few variables of some
persons, the quasi-identifiers (for example age, sex and region), and wants to learn a sensitive
variable of these persons (for example income or a diagnosis). The attacker fits a prediction
model on the release, with the sensitive variable as response and the quasi-identifiers as
predictors, and applies it to the quasi-identifiers of the persons. RAPID is the share of the
original records for which this model puts clearly more probability on the true sensitive value
than an attacker who ignores the quasi-identifiers would [@templ2026rapid].

RAPID therefore measures attribute inference under a declared attacker. It does not measure
re-identification. The attacker never has to find out which released record belongs to which
person. The result depends on three choices, which together make up the attack scenario: the
sensitive variable (`target_var`), the quasi-identifiers (`key_vars`) and the attacker
(`model_type`). They are the arguments of `rapid()` besides the two data sets.

The running example of this vignette has 400 original records with four quasi-identifiers and
two sensitive variables, a numeric income and a categorical health status. The release is an
independent sample from the same model. It contains none of the original records, but it keeps
the dependence of income and health on the quasi-identifiers.

```{r data}
simulate <- function(n) {
  d <- data.frame(
    age = sample(20:69, n, replace = TRUE),
    sex = factor(sample(c("F", "M"), n, replace = TRUE)),
    region = factor(sample(c("north", "south", "east", "west"), n, replace = TRUE)),
    education = factor(sample(c("basic", "secondary", "tertiary"), n,
                              replace = TRUE, prob = c(0.3, 0.5, 0.2)))
  )
  d$income <- round(exp(10.6 + 0.015 * (d$age - 45) + 0.25 * (d$sex == "M") +
                        0.4 * (d$education == "tertiary") -
                        0.25 * (d$education == "basic") + rnorm(n, 0, 0.15)))
  p_chronic <- plogis(-6 + 0.15 * (d$age - 20))
  d$health <- factor(ifelse(runif(n) < p_chronic, "chronic",
                            ifelse(runif(n) < 0.3, "acute", "none")),
                     levels = c("none", "acute", "chronic"))
  d
}
set.seed(2026)
orig <- simulate(400)   # the confidential data
syn  <- simulate(400)   # the release
kv <- c("age", "sex", "region", "education")
head(orig, 3)
```

Region has no effect on either sensitive variable. Income depends on age, sex and education,
and a chronic condition becomes more frequent with age.

# Categorical target: the paper's toy example {#sec-categorical}

When is a correct guess of a class a disclosure? If 60 % of all records are `healthy`, an
attacker who always guesses `healthy` is right for 60 % of these records without knowing
anything about them. RAPID therefore compares the attacker with the marginal distribution of the
original data. For record $i$ with true class $y_i$ it computes three numbers:

* the confidence $g_i$, the probability the attacker's model gives to the true class $y_i$,
* the baseline $b_i = n^{-1} \sum_{j=1}^{n} \mathbf{1}(y_j = y_i)$, the share of the true class
  among the $n$ original records,
* the normalized gain $r_i = (g_i - b_i) / (1 - b_i)$, with $r_i = 0$ where $b_i = 1$.

A gain of 0 means the attacker does no better than the marginal distribution, a gain of 1 means
it is certain of the true class. A record is at risk when $r_i > \tau$, and RAPID is the share of
records at risk. A record at risk is also called flagged. The default threshold is $\tau = 0.3$
(`cat_tau`). The attacker must then cover at least 30 % of the distance between the baseline and
certainty.

The paper's toy example has three records of the class `healthy`, which holds 60 % of the
records, so $b_i = 0.6$ for all three. The attacker gives them the probabilities below.

```{r toy-categorical}
toy <- data.frame(record = 1:3, g = c(0.70, 0.85, 0.55), b = 0.60)
toy$r <- (toy$g - toy$b) / (1 - toy$b)
toy$at_risk <- toy$r > 0.3
toy
mean(toy$at_risk)
```

Record 1 gains `r toy$r[1]` of the possible improvement, which is below the threshold. Record 2
gains `r toy$r[2]` and is at risk. Record 3 does worse than the baseline. RAPID is
`r f3(mean(toy$at_risk))`.

`rapid()` computes the same quantities for every original record. The way a record is flagged is
called the rule. The rule above, the gain over the marginal baseline, has the name
`"RCS_marginal"` in the argument `cat_eval_method` and is the default. Here the attacker is a
random forest, the default `model_type = "rf"`.

The forest and the permutations of [the section on the chance level](#sec-chance) draw random
numbers, and `rapid()` has no default seed. Pass `seed` to make a result reproducible, as all
calls of this vignette do, and report it with the result. Without it two calls differ slightly.
For a linear model only the chance level changes. For a forest the fit is random too, so RAPID
itself can change. [The section on reproducibility](#sec-repro) lists the seed of every function.

```{r health}
r_health <- rapid(orig, syn, key_vars = kv, target_var = "health", seed = 1)
r_health
```

The first line names the attack scenario and the attacker with its settings. The second line gives
the rule. `r r_health$n_at_risk` of the `r r_health$n_total` records are at risk. The chance level
is the share of records that the same predictions flag when they are paired with true values at
random. The excess is RAPID minus the chance level.
[The section on the chance level](#sec-chance) explains both. The mean confidence and baseline per
class show where the risk comes from:

```{r health-by-class}
rec_health <- as.data.frame(r_health)
aggregate(cbind(g, b, at_risk) ~ health, data = rec_health, FUN = mean)
```

A chronic condition holds `r pct(mean(orig$health == "chronic"))` of the original records, and its
baseline is that share. The release lets the attacker see that the condition is frequent among
older persons, so the confidence for it rises far above the baseline. The share at risk is
therefore highest among persons with a chronic condition.

For the class `none` the mean confidence (`r f3(mean(rec_health$g[rec_health$health == "none"]))`)
is close to the baseline (`r f3(mean(rec_health$b[rec_health$health == "none"]))`), and still
`r pct(mean(rec_health$at_risk[rec_health$health == "none"]))` of its records are at risk. The
mean hides groups of different age:

```{r health-none}
rec_none <- rec_health[rec_health$health == "none", ]
rec_none$age_group <- cut(rec_none$age, c(19, 39, 54, 69),
                          labels = c("20-39", "40-54", "55-69"))
by_age <- aggregate(cbind(g, at_risk) ~ age_group, data = rec_none, FUN = mean)
by_age
```

A chronic condition is rare among young persons in the release, so the attacker gives more
probability to `none` for them. Under 40 the mean confidence is `r f3(by_age$g[1])`, and
`r pct(by_age$at_risk[1])` of the persons with `none` are at risk. From 55 on the mean confidence
is `r f3(by_age$g[3])`, below the baseline, and `r pct(by_age$at_risk[3])` of the persons with
`none` are at risk.

# Numeric target: the band {#sec-continuous}

What counts as a correct guess of an income? An exact hit almost never occurs, so RAPID replaces
the true class by a tolerance band around the true value $y_i$,
$$B_i = \{v : e(y_i, v) < \varepsilon\},$$
the open interval of all values within the tolerance $\varepsilon$ (`num_epsilon`) of $y_i$.
The default error $e$ is the symmetric relative error
$e(y, v) = 2|y - v| / (|y| + |v| + 2\delta)$ with the smoothing constant $\delta = 0.01$
(`num_delta`), and the default tolerance is $\varepsilon = 0.1$, that is 10 %.

A model for a numeric target gives more than a point prediction. For a person with given
quasi-identifiers it gives a distribution of plausible incomes, the predictive distribution. The
confidence $g_i$ is now the probability this distribution puts into $B_i$, and the baseline
$b_i = n^{-1} \sum_{j} \mathbf{1}(y_j \in B_i)$ is the share of original values that lie inside
the band. The gain $r_i$ and the condition $r_i > \tau$ are as before, with $\tau = 0.3$
(`num_tau`). The band of a record depends only on its true value and the tolerance, so its
baseline is the same for every attacker.

The paper's toy example uses the symmetric error with $\delta = 0$. For a positive true value
$y$ the band then runs from $y(2 - \varepsilon)/(2 + \varepsilon)$ to
$y(2 + \varepsilon)/(2 - \varepsilon)$. In the paper the attacker's predictive distribution is
given by 100 values, and $g_i$ is the share of them inside the band. The chunk takes the
resulting $g_i$ and $b_i$ from the paper.

```{r toy-numeric}
eps <- 0.1
toy_inc <- data.frame(y = c(50000, 120000, 35000))
toy_inc$band_lo <- toy_inc$y * (2 - eps) / (2 + eps)
toy_inc$band_hi <- toy_inc$y * (2 + eps) / (2 - eps)
toy_inc$g <- c(0.36, 0.60, 0.10)
toy_inc$b <- c(0.30, 0.05, 0.20)
toy_inc$r <- (toy_inc$g - toy_inc$b) / (1 - toy_inc$b)
toy_inc
```

Only record 2 has a gain above 0.3. Its income is rare. A value drawn from the original incomes
lands in its band only `r pct(toy_inc$b[2])` of the time, while the attacker places
`r pct(toy_inc$g[2])` of its distribution there. Record 1 lies near the center of the
distribution, where `r pct(toy_inc$b[1])` of all incomes fall inside the band. The attacker puts
`r pct(toy_inc$g[1])` there, little more than guessing, so the record is not at risk. Suppose the
attacker's point prediction for record 1 is 47000. It lies inside the band, and a rule that looks
only at the point prediction would put the record at risk
([the section on the point rule](#sec-point)).

For the running example the attacker is a linear model. It is fast, and the simulated income is
log-linear in the quasi-identifiers, so it is also a strong attacker here. On real data this is
seldom known. [The section on the attackers](#sec-attackers) says which attacker to choose.

```{r income}
r_inc <- rapid(orig, syn, key_vars = kv, target_var = "income",
               model_type = "lm", seed = 1)
r_inc
```

The attacker line says that the linear model was fitted to the log of income. The argument
`num_scale = "auto"` (default) chooses the log scale when the error metric is relative, all
released values are positive and the log model fits the data better. On the income of this
example the identity scale fits worse and puts fewer records at risk:

```{r lm-scale}
r_identity <- update(r_inc, num_scale = "identity")
r_identity$rapid
```

RAPID is `r f3(r_identity$rapid)` against `r f3(r_inc$rapid)` on the log scale. The record table
holds the band and the three numbers of every record:

```{r income-records}
rec_inc <- as.data.frame(r_inc)
head(rec_inc, 4)
```

Record 1 has an income of `r f0(rec_inc$income[1])`. Its band runs from
`r f0(rec_inc$band_lo[1])` to `r f0(rec_inc$band_hi[1])` and holds `r pct(rec_inc$b[1])` of the
original incomes (`b`). The attacker predicts `r f0(rec_inc$predicted_value[1])` and puts
`r pct(rec_inc$g[1])` of its predictive distribution into the band (`g`). The gain is
`r f3(rec_inc$r[1])`, above the threshold 0.3, so the record is at risk. Record 2 has a rare
income of `r f0(rec_inc$income[2])`, and only `r pct(rec_inc$b[2])` of the original incomes lie in
its band. The attacker predicts `r f0(rec_inc$predicted_value[2])` and puts `r pct(rec_inc$g[2])`
of its distribution into the band, so the gain is `r f3(rec_inc$r[2])`. For record 4 the gain is
`r f3(rec_inc$r[4])`. A negative gain means that the attacker does worse than the baseline. The
column `original_value` repeats the target as it was scored.

The predictive distribution differs by model. The linear model gives a normal (or lognormal)
distribution, a tree the released values in the record's leaf, and a forest the released values in
the record's leaves. `num_dist` chooses whether $g_i$ is computed exactly from it (`"exact"`) or
from 100 quantiles (`"grid"`). The default `"auto"` takes the exact value where the attacker has
one. The section "Attackers" of `?rapid` gives the details, with the quantile regression forest of
@Meinshausen_2006_Quantile for the random forest.

The scenario can also be stored once in a `synth_pair` and reused:

```{r pair}
pair <- synth_pair(orig, syn, key_vars = kv, target_var = "income")
rapid(pair, model_type = "lm", seed = 1)$rapid
```

This is the RAPID of the call with the two data frames above.

# Chance level and excess {#sec-chance}

Is a RAPID of `r f3(r_health$rapid)` for the health status a lot? Some records pass any threshold
by chance. An attacker with concentrated predictions lands near some true values even when the
quasi-identifiers say nothing about the target. To measure this part,
`rapid()` keeps the attacker and its predictions fixed, permutes the true values `n_perm` times
(default 10) and scores each record's prediction against the value it receives, with the baseline
of that value. The chance level is the share of records at risk, averaged over the permutations.
Each permutation scores all $n$ records, so ten permutations give a stable mean.

The excess is RAPID minus the chance level. For the health status the chance level is
`r f3(r_health$chance)` and the excess `r f3(r_health$excess)`. For income under the linear model
RAPID is `r f3(r_inc$rapid)`, the chance level `r f3(r_inc$chance)` and the excess
`r f3(r_inc$excess)`.

The baseline and the chance level correct for different things. The baseline belongs to one
record. It says how often a guess hits the value of this record without any model. The chance
level belongs to the attacker. It says how many records its predictions flag when they are handed
to the wrong persons. A sharp prediction around 50000 fits many persons with an income near 50000,
whoever they are. The chance level therefore depends on the predictions and differs between
attackers and releases.

An excess of `r f3(r_inc$excess)` means that the share of records at risk is
`r sprintf("%.1f", 100 * r_inc$excess)` percentage points above the share that the same
predictions flag under random pairing. Report RAPID, the chance level and the excess together.
When attackers or releases are compared, their chance levels differ, so compare the excess. The
print states that RAPID is not distinguishable from the chance level when the excess is at most
twice the standard deviation of the shares of the permutations.
[The section on testing](#sec-testing) gives a test.

The histogram of the gains shows both parts. The outline is the average histogram of the
gains under the permutations, and the dashed line is the threshold.

```{r plot-gain, fig.cap = "Normalized gains of the original records (bars) and under permuted true values (outline), income, linear model."}
plot(r_inc, which = 1)
```

The bars to the right of the dashed line are the records at risk, `r pct(r_inc$rapid)` of all. The
part of the outline to the right of the line is the chance level, `r pct(r_inc$chance)`. The
excess is the difference. No gain is above `r f3(max(rec_inc$r))`, so the records at risk lie
close to the threshold, and RAPID reacts strongly to the choice of $\tau$ here
([the section on the threshold](#sec-threshold)).

The second plot shows each record's confidence against its baseline. The dotted line $g = b$ marks
a gain of 0. Records above the dashed line $g = b + \tau(1 - b)$ are at risk.

```{r plot-gb, fig.cap = "Confidence g against baseline b per record, income, linear model."}
plot(r_inc, which = 2)
```

The baselines of income lie between `r f3(min(r_inc$baseline))` and
`r f3(max(r_inc$baseline))`. A record in the center of the distribution needs a higher confidence
to be at risk than a record with a rare income.

# Why the point rule misleads {#sec-point}

Why not simply flag a record when the point prediction lies within the tolerance? This was the
rule of riskutility 0.2.0, and it is still available as `num_eval_method = "point"`. It has no
baseline. Near the center of the distribution many values lie within 10 % of the true value, so
any prediction near the center hits the band of many records, whether or not the release carries
information about the target.

To see this, take a release in which the incomes are shuffled. The quasi-identifiers then say
nothing about income, and nothing can be inferred.

```{r shuffled}
syn0 <- syn
syn0$income <- sample(syn0$income)
r_band0  <- rapid(orig, syn0, key_vars = kv, target_var = "income",
                  model_type = "lm", seed = 1)
r_point0 <- rapid(orig, syn0, key_vars = kv, target_var = "income",
                  model_type = "lm", num_eval_method = "point", seed = 1)
r_band0
r_point0
```

The band rule flags `r r_band0$n_at_risk` records, and its chance level is
`r f3(r_band0$chance)`. The linear model finds no dependence and predicts almost the same wide
distribution for everyone. No band holds enough of it to reach the threshold, with the true values
or with permuted ones. The largest confidence is `r f3(max(r_band0$records$g))`.

The point rule flags `r r_point0$n_at_risk` of `r r_point0$n_total` records
(RAPID = `r f3(r_point0$rapid)`), and its chance level is `r f3(r_point0$chance)`. The same
predictions flag about as many records when they are paired with true values at random. Both
prints add that RAPID cannot be distinguished from the chance level. A RAPID of
`r f3(r_point0$rapid)` from the point rule would have been read as a risk in 0.2.0. This is why
the band rule is the default since 0.3.0.

# Working with the result object {#sec-object}

What else does the object hold, and how is it changed? `summary()` adds a confidence interval,
the share of records at risk among those with rare values, and the accuracy of the attacker.

```{r summary}
s_inc <- summary(r_inc)
s_inc
```

The interval is the Wilson interval of `confint()`. The block on rare values takes the
`r s_inc$n_rare` records whose baseline is below its 30 % quantile. Of these,
`r pct(s_inc$rare_hit_rate)` are at risk, against `r pct(r_inc$rapid)` of all records. The last
block describes the point prediction of the attacker for the original records. The relative MAE is
the MAE over the mean absolute income. The prediction misses by
`r pct(r_inc$model_metrics$rmae)` of the mean income on average. The relative RMSE is the RMSE
over the standard deviation of income. A value below 1 means that the attacker predicts better
than the mean income would, and here it is `r f3(r_inc$model_metrics$rrmse)`.

`as.data.frame()` returns the record table, with `at_risk_only = TRUE` only the records at risk.
`nobs()` gives the number of scored records.

```{r records}
nobs(r_inc)
nrow(as.data.frame(r_inc, at_risk_only = TRUE))
```

All `r nobs(r_inc)` records were scored, and `r r_inc$n_at_risk` of them are at risk.

`update()` changes arguments. Where only the rule changes, the stored predictions are rescored
without fitting the model again. Where the attacker or the `seed` changes, the model is refitted,
since the seed also seeds the fit. Both give the same result as a fresh call with the changed
arguments.

```{r update}
r_strict <- update(r_inc, num_tau = 0.4)
c(tau_0.3 = r_inc$rapid, tau_0.4 = r_strict$rapid)
```

With $\tau = 0.4$ RAPID falls from `r f3(r_inc$rapid)` to `r f3(r_strict$rapid)`.

`predict()` applies the attacker to new records, for example persons whose quasi-identifiers an
attacker might know but who are not in the original data. It needs the fitted model, which the
object keeps with `store_model = TRUE`. When the new records include the target, they are scored
with the rule of the object and the baselines of the original values.

```{r predict}
r_model <- update(r_inc, store_model = TRUE)
newcomers <- simulate(3)
pred_new <- predict(r_model, newcomers)
pred_new[, c("age", "sex", "education", "income",
             "predicted_value", "g", "b", "r", "at_risk")]
```

`r sum(pred_new$at_risk)` of the `r nrow(pred_new)` new persons are at risk, although none of them
is in the original data. The linear model has learned how income depends on the
quasi-identifiers, and that knowledge applies to any person of the population.
[The section on the holdout](#sec-holdout) builds on this.

`plot()` has six types. Types 1 and 2 are shown in [the section on the chance level](#sec-chance)
and type 3 in [the section on the threshold](#sec-threshold). Types 4 to 6 show the
quasi-identifiers behind the flags. Type 4 gives their importance in the attacker, and types 5
and 6 give their main effects and pairwise interactions on the flag (`?plot.rapid`). Type 4 needs
the fitted model, so `plot(x, which = 1:6)` stops at type 4 for an object without it. Call
`rapid(..., store_model = TRUE)` from the start. `update(x, store_model = TRUE)` refits the
attacker. For a forest in an object without a seed the result then changes slightly.

# Testing and intervals {#sec-testing}

Is RAPID above its chance level by more than permutation noise? `rapid_test()` permutes the true
values $B$ times (`n_permutations`, default 199), keeps the fitted attacker and computes RAPID
$R_b$ for each permutation. With $R$ the observed RAPID, the p-value is
$p = (1 + \#\{b : R_b \ge R\}) / (1 + B)$. The null hypothesis is that the predictions carry no
information about which true value belongs to which record. The test holds the attacker fixed,
so it needs no refit and is exact given that attacker.

```{r test}
tt <- rapid_test(r_inc, seed = 1)
tt
```

The p-value is `r tt$p_value`. With 199 permutations no p-value can be smaller than
1/200 = 0.005. The chance level in this print, `r f3(tt$chance)`, comes from the 199 permutations
of the test. The `r f3(r_inc$chance)` of `rapid()` comes from its 10 permutations. The print also
gives the Wald test with the statistic
$z = (R - \pi_0) / \sqrt{\pi_0 (1 - \pi_0) / n}$, where $\pi_0$ is the mean of the $R_b$. It needs
a stable estimate of $\pi_0$, so use at least 999 permutations when you report it.

`confint()` gives an interval for RAPID. It treats the $n$ flags as independent given the fitted
attacker. The default is the Wilson interval. `method = "clopper-pearson"` gives the exact
binomial interval, and `"wald"` and `"bootstrap"` are available as well.

```{r confint}
confint(r_inc)
confint(r_inc, method = "clopper-pearson")
```

Both intervals are for RAPID itself. They do not include the uncertainty of the chance level.

# Choosing the threshold {#sec-threshold}

How strict should the threshold be? The tolerance $\varepsilon$ says when a guess counts as a
disclosure. It is a policy choice, made with the target in mind: 10 % is narrow for a target that
varies over orders of magnitude and wide for one with a small relative spread. The absolute
metric (`num_error_metric = "absolute"`) takes the tolerance in the units of the target, for
example 2 years of age, and has no default. The threshold $\tau$ says how much of the possible
gain the attacker must reach. A larger $\tau$ demands more of the attacker, so fewer records are
at risk. The paper uses $\tau = 0.3$ as a reference value for both types of target.

The curve of RAPID over $\tau$, with the chance level at each $\tau$, shows how the result depends
on the choice:

```{r plot-curve, fig.cap = "RAPID and chance level against the threshold tau, income, linear model."}
plot(r_inc, which = 3)
```

The dot marks the threshold in use. The vertical distance between the two curves is the excess at
each threshold. RAPID falls from `r f3(r_inc$rapid)` at $\tau = 0.3$ to `r f3(r_strict$rapid)` at
$\tau = 0.4$. No record has a gain above `r f3(max(rec_inc$r))`, so RAPID is zero for larger
thresholds.

There are two data-driven choices. `threshold_rule = "permutation"` replaces $\tau$ by the
95 % quantile (`perm_level`) of all permuted gains, so that about 5 % of the records or fewer pass
it when the predictions carry no information.

```{r perm-threshold}
r_perm <- update(r_inc, threshold_rule = "permutation")
r_perm$threshold
```

Here the permutation threshold is `r f3(r_perm$threshold)`, and RAPID is `r f3(r_perm$rapid)` at
a chance level of `r f3(r_perm$chance)`. `rapid_threshold_select()` scans a grid of thresholds
(default 0.05 to 0.95) and compares RAPID at each with the 95 % quantile of its permutation
distribution. It returns the largest threshold at which RAPID is still above that quantile. This
is the most demanding threshold at which the attacker still flags more records than chance.

```{r threshold-select}
ts <- rapid_threshold_select(r_inc, seed = 1)
ts
```

Above $\tau$ = `r ts$threshold_star` no threshold is significant. The gain of a record is below
its confidence, and the confidence of the linear model never exceeds `r f3(max(r_inc$records$g))`
here (see the plot of $g$ against $b$). Thresholds near that value flag almost no record. Each
threshold of the grid is tested on its own, without a correction for testing many. The
recommended threshold is exploratory: it describes how demanding a threshold can be before the
signal is lost. A test with `rapid_test()` at this threshold on the same data is not a
confirmation, because the threshold was chosen by looking at these data. To test a threshold, fix
it in advance, or select it on one data set and test it on data not used for the selection, such
as a holdout or another release.

Which of the three to use? Keep the fixed threshold 0.3 for a result that is compared with other
releases or with the paper. Use the permutation threshold to hold the share of records flagged
without information at about 5 %. Use `rapid_threshold_select()` to explore how far the signal
reaches.

# Holdout and release-specific risk {#sec-holdout}

How much of RAPID is due to the persons whose records were used for the release? The records of
a holdout come from the same population but were not used to generate the release. `rapid()`
scores them with the same attacker and rule. Their RAPID measures inference from the
quasi-identifiers alone, the risk that any faithful release carries for any person of the
population. The difference `release_specific`, RAPID minus holdout RAPID, is the part that is
specific to the records behind the release.

The data holder sets the holdout aside before the synthesis. Records that went into the release
cannot serve as a holdout afterwards. Without a holdout,
[`rapid_synthesizer_cv()`](#sec-cv) gives the same kind of information for the method.

To see both parts, consider a second release that is an exact copy of the first 300 original
records. Records 301 to 400 were not used for it and serve as the holdout. Two attackers are
applied. The first is the linear model of the sections above. The second is the lookup attacker
(`model_type = "lookup"`), one fully grown tree that reads off the released records with the same
values of the quasi-identifiers. [The next section](#sec-attackers) compares it with other
attackers.

```{r holdout}
released <- orig[1:300, ]
holdout  <- orig[301:400, ]
attack_copy <- function(...) {
  rapid(released, released, key_vars = kv, target_var = "income",
        holdout = holdout, seed = 1, ...)
}
fits <- list(lm = attack_copy(model_type = "lm"),
             lookup = attack_copy(model_type = "lookup"))
fits$lm
fits$lookup
```

Each print has two more lines. The first gives RAPID, the chance level and the excess on the
holdout records, and the second the release-specific part. For the linear model the
release-specific part is `r f3(fits$lm$release_specific)`. An attacker that cannot reproduce
records has a release-specific part near zero, so this value is noise. A share near
`r f3(fits$lm$holdout$rapid)` estimated from `r fits$lm$holdout$n` records has a standard error of
about `r f3(sqrt(fits$lm$holdout$rapid * (1 - fits$lm$holdout$rapid) / fits$lm$holdout$n))`. The
lookup attacker flags `r f3(fits$lookup$rapid)` of the copied records and
`r f3(fits$lookup$holdout$rapid)` of the holdout records. Its release-specific part,
`r f3(fits$lookup$release_specific)`, is the trace of the copy. A holdout can also be stored in a
`synth_pair` with `synth_pair(..., holdout = )`.

# Inference and reproduction: which attacker answers which question {#sec-attackers}

Does it matter which model the attacker uses? It does, and the attackers answer different
questions. The copied release of [the section on the holdout](#sec-holdout) shows this. The chunk
adds three random forests and a pruned tree to the two attackers fitted there.

```{r copy}
fits$rf_node_1  <- attack_copy(model_type = "rf", min.node.size = 1)
fits$rf_node_5  <- attack_copy(model_type = "rf")
fits$rf_node_20 <- attack_copy(model_type = "rf", min.node.size = 20)
if (has_rpart) fits$cart <- attack_copy(model_type = "cart")
```

The table collects `rapid`, `chance`, `excess`, `holdout$rapid` and `release_specific` of each
fitted object.

```{r copy-table, echo = FALSE}
fits <- fits[intersect(c("lm", "cart", "rf_node_20", "rf_node_5", "rf_node_1", "lookup"),
                       names(fits))]
copy_table <- data.frame(
  attacker = vapply(fits, function(x) x$attacker, ""),
  rapid = vapply(fits, function(x) x$rapid, 0),
  chance = vapply(fits, function(x) x$chance, 0),
  excess = vapply(fits, function(x) x$excess, 0),
  holdout = vapply(fits, function(x) x$holdout$rapid, 0),
  release_specific = vapply(fits, function(x) x$release_specific, 0)
)
# standard error of the difference of two independent shares (300 and 100 records)
se_diff <- function(x) {
  sqrt(x$rapid * (1 - x$rapid) / x$n_total +
       x$holdout$rapid * (1 - x$holdout$rapid) / x$holdout$n)
}
copy_table$se_diff <- vapply(fits, se_diff, 0)
knitr::kable(copy_table, digits = 3,
             caption = "RAPID on a copied release (records 1 to 300) and on the holdout.")
```

```{r copy-text, include = FALSE}
cart_text <- if (has_rpart) {
  sprintf(paste("It flags %s of the copied records and %s of the holdout records. The",
                "difference, %s, is %.1f standard errors, so this example does not settle",
                "whether the pruned tree also picks up the copied records."),
          f3(fits$cart$rapid), f3(fits$cart$holdout$rapid),
          f3(fits$cart$release_specific),
          fits$cart$release_specific / se_diff(fits$cart))
} else {
  "The package rpart is not installed, so the tree was not fitted here."
}
```

The column `se_diff` is the standard error of the release-specific part when the flags are treated
as independent, as `confint()` does.

*Generalizing attackers* learn how the target depends on the quasi-identifiers. Their RAPID
measures inference from the quasi-identifiers, which any release that keeps the dependence
allows, for the persons in the original data and for others alike. The linear model is one of
them. It has a handful of parameters and cannot reproduce single records. Its release-specific
part is `r sprintf("%.1f", abs(fits$lm$release_specific) / se_diff(fits$lm))` standard errors from
zero, so the linear model does not tell the copied records from the others. The tree of
`model_type = "cart"` is pruned by cross-validation, which moves it towards the generalizing
end. `r cart_text`

The *lookup attacker* measures whether the release reproduces the values of the records. Its
release-specific part is `r sprintf("%.0f", fits$lookup$release_specific / se_diff(fits$lookup))`
standard errors from zero. Most leaves of the lookup tree hold a single released value. The
confidence is then 0 or 1, as it is for `r pct(mean(fits$lookup$records$g %in% c(0, 1)))` of the
copied records, and a record is flagged whenever that one value falls into its band. Under random
pairing this happens about as often as the mean baseline says
(`r f3(mean(fits$lookup$baseline))`), and the chance level is `r f3(fits$lookup$chance)`. On the
holdout records, which the release does not contain, the lookup attacker still flags
`r f3(fits$lookup$holdout$rapid)`. Its RAPID is therefore well above zero for any release with
plausible values. Read its excess, and with a holdout its release-specific part. The print adds a
line that says so.

The *random forest* lies between the two, and where it lies depends on ranger's minimum node size
`min.node.size`. `rapid()` leaves it at ranger's default (5 for a numeric target, 10 for class
probabilities) and reports it in the attacker line. With node size 1 the forest flags
`r f3(fits$rf_node_1$rapid)` of the copied records and `r f3(fits$rf_node_1$holdout$rapid)` of the
holdout records. With node size 20 it flags `r f3(fits$rf_node_20$rapid)` and
`r f3(fits$rf_node_20$holdout$rapid)`. The release-specific part shrinks with the node size, from
`r f3(fits$rf_node_1$release_specific)` to `r f3(fits$rf_node_20$release_specific)`. `?rapid`
(section "Attackers") gives the same comparison for a target that does not depend on the
quasi-identifiers, where every record at risk beyond chance is a reproduced record. There the
result also depends on ranger's `mtry`: with its default the forest did not detect an exact copy,
and it did when all quasi-identifiers were tried at every split.

A small RAPID or a small excess under one attacker does not show that the release is safe. It
shows that this attacker, with these quasi-identifiers and this rule, infers little. A copied
release looks no riskier to the linear model than an independent release. On the copy it flags
`r f3(fits$lm$rapid)` of the records, on the independent release of the running example
`r f3(r_inc$rapid)`.

Which attacker to choose depends on the question:

| Your question | Attacker | Read |
|---------------|----------|------|
| What can be inferred from the quasi-identifiers, for any person of the population? | `"lm"` (numeric target), `"logit"` (two classes), `"cart"` | RAPID, chance level, excess |
| Does the release reproduce values of original records? | `"lookup"`, or `"rf"` with `min.node.size = 1`, with a `holdout` | excess and `release_specific` |
| A first look without a specific question | `"rf"` (default) | RAPID and excess. Add a `holdout` to separate the two parts |
| A result for a report | `rapid_suite()` | the largest excess |

# Model suite and worst case {#sec-suite}

Which attacker should be reported? The paper recommends a suite of attackers, summarized by the
worst case. `rapid_suite()` fits one `rapid()` object per attacker with the same arguments and
seed. Its default suite is random forest, pruned tree, gradient boosting and lookup attacker
(`model_types = c("rf", "cart", "gbm", "lookup")`). Gradient boosting needs the package xgboost
and the tree needs rpart. An attacker whose package is missing is skipped with a warning. Here the
suite runs the attackers that need no further package:

```{r suite}
suite <- rapid_suite(orig, syn, key_vars = kv, target_var = "income",
                     model_types = c("lm", "rf", "lookup"), seed = 1)
suite
```

On the independent release the largest RAPID is `r f3(suite$rapid_max)` (`r suite$worst_model`),
and the largest excess `r f3(suite$excess_max)` (`r suite$worst_model_excess`). With a lookup
attacker in the suite, compare the attackers by their excess, as the print says.
`rapid_suite(r1, r2)` also combines `rapid` objects fitted before, if they share the scenario and
the rule.

```{r plot-suite, fig.cap = "RAPID and chance level of each attacker of the suite."}
plot(suite)
```

For each attacker the distance between the triangle and the dot is the excess. The worst case
covers only the attackers in the suite. A small maximum under three attackers is no proof that a
fourth one would infer as little.

# Contribution of the quasi-identifiers {#sec-qi}

Which quasi-identifier carries the risk? `rapid_qi_contribution()` removes one quasi-identifier at
a time from the attacker's knowledge, refits the attacker and records the drop in RAPID and in
the excess. The argument `groups` drops sets of quasi-identifiers that carry the same
information together. The chance level of each scenario comes from `n_permutations`
permutations (default 99, 19 here to keep the vignette fast).

```{r qi}
qi <- rapid_qi_contribution(orig, syn, key_vars = kv, target_var = "income",
                            model_type = "lm", n_permutations = 19, seed = 1)
qi
```

Without age or without education the linear model flags no record at all. Without sex RAPID falls
to `r f3(qi$results$rapid[qi$results$dropped == "sex"])`. Removing region changes almost nothing,
as the simulation intended. A small drop means that the quasi-identifier is not needed given the
others. It does not mean that it is harmless on its own. With one release, differences of a few
thousandths are within the noise of the fit.

# Cross-validation of a synthesizer {#sec-cv}

How risky is a synthesis method, as opposed to one release of it? `rapid_synthesizer_cv()` splits
the original data into `k` folds (default 5), trains the synthesizer on all folds but one, and
computes RAPID on the left-out fold. The synthesizer is any function that takes a data frame
(and optionally a `seed`) and returns a synthetic one. The default is `synthpop::syn()`. Here a
simple parametric synthesizer stands in for it. It regresses log income on the
quasi-identifiers and draws new incomes from the fit.

```{r cv}
parametric_syn <- function(data, seed = NULL) {
  if (!is.null(seed)) set.seed(seed)
  fit <- lm(log(income) ~ age + sex + education, data = data)
  data$income <- round(exp(fitted(fit) + rnorm(nrow(data), 0, sigma(fit))))
  data
}
cv <- rapid_synthesizer_cv(orig[, c(kv, "income")], synthesizer = parametric_syn,
                           key_vars = kv, target_var = "income",
                           model_type = "lm", seed = 1)
cv
```

The folds give a mean RAPID of `r f3(cv$rapid)` with a mean chance level of `r f3(cv$chance)`. The
interval is a t interval of the mean of the `r cv$settings$k` fold values,
mean $\pm$ `qt(0.975, k - 1)` sd / $\sqrt{k}$. With `r cv$settings$k` folds it reaches
`r sprintf("%.2f", qt(0.975, cv$settings$k - 1))` standard errors to each side. It is a rough
guide, because the folds share the original data. The fold values come from records the
synthesizer has not seen, so they measure the inference that the method transmits, like the
holdout in [the section on the holdout](#sec-holdout). Once a method is chosen, compute RAPID on
the final release.

# Your own attacker {#sec-learner}

What if the attacker you want to declare is not among the built-in ones? `rapid_learner()` builds
one from functions. `fit(formula, data)` trains it on the release. For a numeric target,
`predict_point(fit, newdata)` gives a point prediction and `predict_quantiles(fit, newdata, probs)`
the predictive distribution as quantiles, which the band rule needs. For a categorical target,
`predict_prob(fit, newdata)` gives the class probabilities. The functions are called with their
arguments by position, in this order.

The attacker below fits a linear model to the log of the target and takes its predictive
distribution from the empirical quantiles of the residuals instead of a normal distribution.

```{r learner}
log_lm <- rapid_learner(
  "log_lm",
  fit = function(formula, data) lm(update(formula, log(.) ~ .), data = data),
  predict_point = function(fit, newdata) exp(predict(fit, newdata)),
  predict_quantiles = function(fit, newdata, probs) {
    q <- quantile(residuals(fit), probs, names = FALSE)
    exp(outer(predict(fit, newdata), q, "+"))
  }
)
r_own <- rapid(orig, syn, key_vars = kv, target_var = "income",
               model_type = log_lm, seed = 1)
r_own
```

It gives RAPID `r f3(r_own$rapid)`, close to the `r f3(r_inc$rapid)` of the built-in linear model
on the log scale. A user-defined attacker can be used wherever `model_type` is accepted, also in
`rapid_suite()`, `rapid_qi_contribution()` and `rapid_synthesizer_cv()`.

# In practice {#sec-practice}

This section is for the reader who comes back with one question. It maps the questions to the
functions and collects what a report needs and what goes wrong most often.

## Which function for which question {#sec-which}

| Question | Call | Section |
|----------|------|---------|
| For how many records can the attacker infer the value? | `rapid()` | [Categorical target](#sec-categorical), [numeric target](#sec-continuous) |
| Is that more than chance? | `chance` and `excess` in the print, `rapid_test()` | [Chance level](#sec-chance), [testing](#sec-testing) |
| How uncertain is RAPID? | `confint()` | [Testing](#sec-testing) |
| Which records are at risk? | `as.data.frame(x, at_risk_only = TRUE)` | [Result object](#sec-object) |
| How does the result depend on the threshold? | `plot(x, which = 3)`, `update(x, num_tau = )` | [Threshold](#sec-threshold) |
| Does the release reproduce original records? | `holdout =`, `model_type = "lookup"` | [Holdout](#sec-holdout), [attackers](#sec-attackers) |
| Does the result depend on the attacker? | `rapid_suite()` | [Model suite](#sec-suite) |
| Which quasi-identifier carries the risk? | `rapid_qi_contribution()` | [Quasi-identifiers](#sec-qi) |
| How risky is the synthesis method? | `rapid_synthesizer_cv()` | [Cross-validation](#sec-cv) |
| What about persons outside the data? | `predict()` with `store_model = TRUE` | [Result object](#sec-object) |
| An attacker that is not built in? | `rapid_learner()` | [Your own attacker](#sec-learner) |

## Reading a result {#sec-reading}

Is the release risky? The sections above give the pieces of an answer. Read them in this order.

1. Look at the excess first. It is the share of records the attacker infers beyond random
   pairing. `rapid_test()` says whether the excess differs from 0. It does not say whether the
   excess is large.
2. Ask where the excess comes from. With a holdout, the excess on the holdout records is
   inference that any person of the population is exposed to, because the release keeps the
   dependence of the target on the quasi-identifiers. `release_specific` is what the records
   behind the release carry in addition.
3. Without a holdout, compare a generalizing attacker (`"lm"`, `"cart"`) with the lookup
   attacker. An excess under the lookup attacker that the generalizing attacker does not show
   points to reproduced records. On the copied release the excess is `r f3(fits$lookup$excess)`
   under the lookup attacker and `r f3(fits$lm$excess)` under the linear model. On the
   independent release the two are `r f3(suite$fits[["lookup"]]$excess)` and
   `r f3(suite$fits[["lm"]]$excess)`.

There is no general cut-off. A small excess under the attackers tried does not show that the
release is safe.

## Reporting a result {#sec-report}

A RAPID value has no meaning without its scenario. A report states

* the sensitive variable and the quasi-identifiers,
* the attacker with its settings (the attacker line of the print),
* the rule: error metric, tolerance and threshold,
* RAPID with its interval, the chance level, the excess and the number of scored records,
* the p-value of `rapid_test()` with the number of permutations,
* the seed and the version of riskutility.

For the running example:

> Attribute disclosure risk of `r r_inc$target_var` given
> `r knitr::combine_words(r_inc$key_vars, oxford_comma = FALSE)` was measured with RAPID
> (riskutility `r as.character(packageVersion("riskutility"))`, seed `r r_inc$seed`). The rule
> was the band rule with a `r r_inc$rule$metric` relative tolerance of
> `r 100 * r_inc$rule$epsilon` % and a gain threshold of `r r_inc$rule$threshold`. Under a linear
> model on the log scale `r r_inc$n_at_risk` of `r nobs(r_inc)` records were at risk,
> RAPID = `r f3(r_inc$rapid)` (95 % Wilson interval `r f3(confint(r_inc)[1])` to
> `r f3(confint(r_inc)[2])`). The chance level was `r f3(r_inc$chance)` (`r r_inc$n_perm`
> permutations) and the excess `r f3(r_inc$excess)` (permutation test, `r tt$n_permutations`
> permutations, p = `r tt$p_value`).

With several attackers, report the table of `rapid_suite()` and name the attacker with the
largest excess.

## Missing values {#sec-missing}

What happens to records without a target value? For a numeric target they are removed by
default (`na_strategy = "drop"`), with a warning, and RAPID is the share among the records with
an observed target.

```{r missing}
orig_na <- orig
orig_na$income[c(3, 7, 9)] <- NA
r_na <- rapid(orig_na, syn, key_vars = kv, target_var = "income",
              model_type = "lm", seed = 1)
nobs(r_na)
```

RAPID now refers to `r nobs(r_na)` records. State this number in a report.
`na_strategy = "constant"` and `"median"` keep the records and score them against a replaced
value. A missing value of a categorical target becomes the level `"missing"`, with a warning, and
the record stays in the count. A missing value of a categorical quasi-identifier becomes the
level `"missing"` as well. A linear model stops with an error when this level does not occur in
the release. The forest accepts it. A numeric quasi-identifier with missing values is an error.
Impute it or drop the records before the call. `?rapid` (section "Missing values") has the
details.

## Reproducibility {#sec-repro}

A result is reproducible when every random step has a seed.
[The section on the categorical target](#sec-categorical) says what is random in `rapid()`. The
table lists the seed of every step.

| Step | What is random | Seed |
|------|----------------|------|
| `rapid()` | the fit of the forest, the cross-validation of the pruned tree, and the permutations | `seed` |
| `update()`, `plot()` | the permutations | the seed of the object |
| `rapid_test()`, `rapid_threshold_select()` on an object | the permutations | their own `seed`. The seed of the object is not used |
| `confint(method = "bootstrap")` | the resampling | its own `seed` |
| `rapid_suite()`, `rapid_qi_contribution()` | every fit and its permutations | `seed`, the same for every fit |
| `rapid_synthesizer_cv()` | the folds, the synthesizer and the fits | `seed` |

`set.seed()` before a call without `seed` works as well. The linear model has no random fit, so
only its permutations are random. A forest with a seed gave the same result with 1 and with 4
threads (`num.threads`).

## Pitfalls {#sec-pitfalls}

* No default seed. Pass `seed` and report it ([reproducibility](#sec-repro)).
* Missing target values are removed by default, which changes the number of scored records
  ([missing values](#sec-missing)).
* A threshold from `rapid_threshold_select()` is exploratory. Do not test at it on the same data
  ([choosing the threshold](#sec-threshold)).
* A small RAPID under one attacker is a statement about that attacker. A copied release looks no
  riskier to a linear model than an independent one ([attackers](#sec-attackers)).
* Read the lookup attacker by its excess ([attackers](#sec-attackers)).
* The same tolerance does not make RAPID comparable across targets. 10 % is narrow for a target
  that varies over orders of magnitude and wide for one with a small relative spread.
* A wide predictive distribution cannot reach the threshold. RAPID = 0 can then mean that the
  tolerance is narrow relative to the attacker's error. Check the largest `g`
  (`max(x$records$g)`) and plot type 2.

The last point can be checked with a bound. For the linear model on the log scale with residual
standard deviation `s`, the confidence is at most about `2 * pnorm(epsilon / s) - 1`.

```{r bound}
s <- sigma(r_model$model)
c(s = s, bound = 2 * pnorm(0.1 / s) - 1, largest_g = max(r_inc$records$g))
```

In the running example the bound is `r f3(2 * pnorm(0.1 / s) - 1)` and the largest confidence
`r f3(max(r_inc$records$g))`. A record with baseline `b` is at risk when its confidence is above
`b + tau * (1 - b)`, which is `r f3(max(r_inc$baseline) + 0.3 * (1 - max(r_inc$baseline)))` for
the largest baseline of income. The linear model can reach this value here. With `s = 0.25` the
bound would be `r f3(2 * pnorm(0.1 / 0.25) - 1)`, and only a record with a baseline below
`r f3((2 * pnorm(0.1 / 0.25) - 1 - 0.3) / 0.7)` could be at risk. RAPID = 0 then says that the
tolerance is narrow relative to the attacker's error. It does not show that the quasi-identifiers
carry no information.

# Migration from 0.2.0 {#sec-migration}

Which results change, and how do you get the old ones? Release 0.3.0 changes the default rules,
so a call that ran in 0.2.0 gives a different value now. Each line below gives a call of 0.2.0
and the call that gives the same rule in 0.3.0 (`?rapid`, section "Changes in 0.3.0").

| 0.2.0 | 0.3.0 equivalent |
|-------|------------------|
| `rapid(X, Y, kv, tv)`, numeric target | `rapid(X, Y, kv, tv, num_eval_method = "point", num_epsilon = 0.1)` |
| `num_epsilon = 10` (percent) | `num_epsilon = 0.1` (proportion) |
| `num_epsilon_type = "absolute", num_epsilon = 2` | `num_error_metric = "absolute", num_epsilon = 2` |
| `rapid(X, Y, kv, tv)`, categorical target | `rapid(X, Y, kv, tv, cat_eval_method = "RCS_conditional")` |
| `model_type = "lm"` | `model_type = "lm", num_scale = "identity"` |
| `model_type = "cart"` | `model_type = "cart", prune = FALSE, cp = 0.01, minsplit = 20, minbucket = 7` |
| `rapid(X, Y, kv, tv)`, numeric target with missing values | `rapid(X, Y, kv, tv, na_strategy = "constant")` |
| `return_all_records = FALSE` | `as.data.frame(x, at_risk_only = TRUE)` |
| `rapid(original_data = X, synthetic_data = Y, quasi_identifiers = kv, sensitive_attribute = tv)` | unchanged, the old names are aliases |

For the random forest, the default attacker, no attacker setting changed. With the same random
stream (`set.seed()` before the call in 0.2.0, the same `set.seed()` or `seed =` in 0.3.0) and
the point rule of the first line, the value of 0.2.0 is reproduced.

The risk levels LOW, MEDIUM and HIGH of `summary()` are gone. Read the excess over the chance
level and `rapid_test()` instead ([reading a result](#sec-reading)). `rumap()` now reports the
excess of a random forest attacker, `max(0, rapid - chance)`, and `disclosure_report()` passes
RAPID when the p-value of `rapid_test()` is above `rapid_alpha` (default 0.05). For a release
under the point rule, `rapid_threshold_select()` now recommends the smallest significant
tolerance, which is the strictest. `NEWS.md` lists all changes.

# Reproducing the paper {#sec-paper}

How do you get the numbers of the paper? The RAPID paper [@templ2026rapid] and the RAPID package
of Oscar Thees use the band rule with the defaults of this vignette and three settings that
differ from the defaults here: `num_dist = "grid"` (every predictive distribution as 100
quantiles), `num_scale = "identity"` (the linear model on the scale of the target) and, for the
tree, `prune = FALSE, cp = 0.01, minsplit = 20, minbucket = 7` (the rpart defaults without
pruning). `minsplit` must be given, because with `minbucket = 7` alone rpart sets
`minsplit = 21`. `?rapid` has the section "Reproducing the paper and the RAPID package".

```{r paper-settings, eval = has_rpart}
rapid(orig, syn, key_vars = kv, target_var = "income", model_type = "cart",
      num_dist = "grid", prune = FALSE, cp = 0.01, minsplit = 20, minbucket = 7,
      seed = 1)
```

The attacker line shows that the tree is not pruned. With these settings the results for the
linear model and the tree agree with those of the RAPID package. The results for the forest and
gradient boosting agree up to the random draws of the two implementations.
